prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength bring time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the optical lattice clock as my preferred single-part prize. The scientific case has not weakened: the magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift on the clock transition for many neutral atoms at once, and the realisation of 1e-18 accuracy and stability, with controlled many-body effects, has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories and compared over fibre links. The chair asked whether this is a third recognition in the metrology lineage (2005 comb, 2012 ion control). My answer is that it is a separate achievement: the comb supplies the means to count optical cycles, ion control supplies a single-particle reference, and the lattice clock solves the different problem of interrogating a large ensemble without perturbing the transition, which is where the stability comes from. The two-name credit has no forced omission within the supplied names, which is rare on this shortlist. On the pending redefinition of the second, I treat it as a timing signal and not as a criterion of physics merit; independent clocks already agree, and that agreement is the evidence of maturity. A citation should name the lattice-clock concept and its precision realisation, not clocks in general, and should describe Ye's part as precision and many-body control, not only as demonstration, as Kroll asked.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that attribution is clean only inside the supplied names. Ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat and others) lie outside the credit, and the lineage argument will not persuade every colleague. The weight of this candidate beyond metrology is also narrower than that of B039: a better clock changes what can be measured, but band topology changed how a whole class of phases is classified, and I do not dismiss that. The chair asked whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission outweighs the B039 chain. It does not make B039 weak science, but it is a visible gap in the credit that I cannot see how to repair within the supplied names, and a citation scoped to the 2D case reduces but does not remove it. I would support B039 with that scoped citation as a second choice and would not regard its award as a mistake.

responses.point: Placed B039 first as a clear Kane-Mele-to-Molenkamp chain, arguing that its conceptual reach exceeds that of a better clock, that it extends the 2016 prize to time-reversal-invariant materials, and that credit gaps apply to almost every candidate including the clock.
responses.response: I agree that credit gaps are general, and that is why I weigh the size of the gap, not its existence. For the clock, what stands outside the two names is other groups working on the same idea and an earlier lineage already honoured. For B039, what stands outside is the HgTe prediction that the credited experiment tested and the whole 3D programme. I accept your reading that the topological case extends the 2016 prize rather than repeating it, and I accept that the conceptual reach of band topology is larger. Where I still differ is that, for a committee limited to three names, the clock gives the more defensible allocation. I would be content with your scoped 2D citation if the committee chooses B039.

responses.point: Ranked B039 first, treating it as mature and arguably overdue and arguing that the topological-insulator field should be recognised once, not split across two parts.
responses.response: I agree that the field should be treated as one prize and I would not add a second topological part to any configuration, so my preferred configuration has none. You have also pressed the point about maturity, and I concede that about two decades of confirmation across transport, photoemission and scanning probes is a stronger record than the clock has in terms of breadth of platforms. My remaining difference is about what the credit can bear: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction guided Molenkamp's experiment, and Zhang is no longer living, so that omission cannot be mended later. If the committee accepts a 2D-scoped citation I would not oppose it, but I do not think the allocation problem disappears because the wording is narrowed.

responses.point: Ranked B022 first and argues the redefinition of the SI second is irrelevant to merit, that neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping is distinct from 2005 and 2012, and that Ye's role should be described as precision and many-body control.
responses.response: I agree on distinctness and on the wording of Ye's contribution, and I have adopted precision realisation in the citation. I differ slightly on the redefinition: I do not treat it as a merit criterion either, but I would not say it is irrelevant to timing, because a committee may reasonably prefer to wait for the metrology bodies if it judged the evidence otherwise equal. I would also take more seriously than you do the point that topological insulators have had wider influence across condensed matter; I rank the clock first on the cleaner credit and on its clear measurable consequence, not on a claim of greater reach.

responses.point: Proposes a two-part prize pairing the lattice clock (Katori, Ye) with IceCube neutrinos (Halzen alone) for three laureates in total.
responses.response: I appreciate that you support the clock, and I accept that the diffuse flux is a real discovery. I cannot support adding B003, because you identify the one-name credit for a collaboration-scale result as the weakest part of your own configuration, AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal pioneers stay outside it, and the origin of most of the flux is unidentified. Adding it would weaken a clean two-name prize with a part whose credit I do not think the committee can defend. If the committee wants a two-part prize, I would want a better-grounded second part than this one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or sees it as a third recognition in one lineage.
How the committee would weigh the other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups against Katori and Ye, given that the credit cannot be extended.
Whether a 2D-scoped B039 citation keeps the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from reading as a dismissal; I rely on recollection for this priority history and have not verified it.
I have not independently verified specific record accuracy and stability figures for individual clocks.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile documents collaborations with Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich and others, but none of the shortlisted credited names appears among them, so no specific conflict is apparent. My field proximity as an atomic theorist (atomic structure relevant to clock transitions and to ultracold-atom and trapped-ion platforms) is a disclosure about expertise, not a personal connection. I see no recusal ground for B022, B039 or B005.
